messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Identifiability in Confirmatory Factor Analsysis
parts:
I'm continuing to delve into how to use Stan for Structural Equation Modelling, and I've figured out how to replicate the confirmatory factor analysis of the "HolzingerSwineford1939" data set from the lavaan package (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cfa.html). Here's the Stan code:

data{

  #N: number of subjects
  int N ;

  #K: number of outcomes per subject
  int K ;

  #Y: matrix of outcomes
  matrix[N,K] Y ;

}
transformed data{

  # zeroesForFacMeans: vector of zeroes for factor means
  vector[3] zeroesForFacMeans ;
  zeroesForFacMeans = rep_vector(0,3) ;

}
parameters{

  # facSds: SDs for the 3 latent factors
  vector<lower=0>[3] facSds ;

  # facCor: correlations amongst the 3 latent factors
  corr_matrix[3] facCor ;

  # subjFacs: matrix of values for each factor associated with each subject
  matrix[N,3] subjFacs ;

  # outcomeMeans: means for each outcome
  vector[9] outcomeMeans ;

  # outcomeSds: SDs for each outcome
  vector<lower=0>[9] outcomeSds ;

  # betas: how each factor loads on to each outcome.
  #        only 6 (rather than 9) because first beta
  #        for each factor set has been fixed at 1
  #        for identifiability
  vector[6] betas ;

}
transformed parameters{

  #facCov: covariance matrix for latent factors
  matrix[3,3] facCov ;
  facCov = quad_form_diag(facCor,facSds) ;

}
model{

  #priors, assumes data have been scale()ed
  facSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
  facCor ~ lkj_corr(1) ;
  outcomeMeans ~ normal(0,1) ;
  outcomeSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
  betas ~ normal(0,1) ;

  #generative model:
  for(i in 1:N){
    subjFacs[i] ~ multi_normal(zeroesForFacMeans,facCov) ;
    Y[i,1] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]          + outcomeMeans[1] , outcomeSds[1] ) ;
    Y[i,2] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[1] + outcomeMeans[2] , outcomeSds[2] ) ;
    Y[i,3] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[2] + outcomeMeans[3] , outcomeSds[3] ) ;
    Y[i,4] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]          + outcomeMeans[4] , outcomeSds[4] ) ;
    Y[i,5] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]*betas[3] + outcomeMeans[5] , outcomeSds[5] ) ;
    Y[i,6] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]*betas[4] + outcomeMeans[6] , outcomeSds[6] ) ;
    Y[i,7] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]          + outcomeMeans[7] , outcomeSds[7] ) ;
    Y[i,8] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]*betas[5] + outcomeMeans[8] , outcomeSds[8] ) ;
    Y[i,9] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]*betas[6] + outcomeMeans[9] , outcomeSds[9] ) ;
  }

}




Using this, I get results that are fairly similar to those reported in the lavaan tutorial. As you can see, this version of the model ensures identifiability by fixing the first beta (is it correct to call this the "loading"?) for each outcome set to 1. However, I'd like to try a version that instead ensures identifiability by fixing the SDs of the latent factors to 1, but when I attempt this, I get very poor sampling (takes a long time to get even a small ESS). Presumably I have misunderstood something?

Here's the code for this second version:

data{

  #N: number of subjects
  int N ;

  #K: number of outcomes per subject
  int K ;

  #Y: matrix of outcomes
  matrix[N,K] Y ;

}
transformed data{

  # zeroesForFacMeans: vector of zeroes for factor means
  vector[3] zeroesForFacMeans ;
  zeroesForFacMeans = rep_vector(0,3) ;

}
parameters{

  # facCor: correlations amongst the 3 latent factors
  corr_matrix[3] facCor ;

  # subjFacs: matrix of values for each factor associated with each subject
  matrix[N,3] subjFacs ;

  # outcomeMeans: means for each outcome
  vector[9] outcomeMeans ;

  # outcomeSds: SDs for each outcome
  vector<lower=0>[9] outcomeSds ;

  # betas: how each factor loads on to each outcome.
  vector[9] betas ;

}
model{

  #priors, assumes data have been scale()ed
  facCor ~ lkj_corr(1) ;
  outcomeMeans ~ normal(0,1) ;
  outcomeSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
  betas ~ normal(0,1) ;

  #generative model:
  for(i in 1:N){
    subjFacs[i] ~ multi_normal(zeroesForFacMeans,facCor) ;
    Y[i,1] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[1] + outcomeMeans[1] , outcomeSds[1] ) ;
    Y[i,2] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[2] + outcomeMeans[2] , outcomeSds[2] ) ;
    Y[i,3] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[3] + outcomeMeans[3] , outcomeSds[3] ) ;
    Y[i,4] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]*betas[4] + outcomeMeans[4] , outcomeSds[4] ) ;
    Y[i,5] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]*betas[5] + outcomeMeans[5] , outcomeSds[5] ) ;
    Y[i,6] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,2]*betas[6] + outcomeMeans[6] , outcomeSds[6] ) ;
    Y[i,7] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]*betas[7] + outcomeMeans[7] , outcomeSds[7] ) ;
    Y[i,8] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]*betas[8] + outcomeMeans[8] , outcomeSds[8] ) ;
    Y[i,9] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,3]*betas[9] + outcomeMeans[9] , outcomeSds[9] ) ;
  }

}

On Wednesday, November 16, 2016 at 2:40:27 PM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
Using this, I get results that are fairly similar to those reported in the lavaan tutorial. As you can see, this version of the model ensures identifiability by fixing the first beta (is it correct to call this the "loading"?) for each outcome set to 1. However, I'd like to try a version that instead ensures identifiability by fixing the SDs of the latent factors to 1, but when I attempt this, I get very poor sampling (takes a long time to get even a small ESS). Presumably I have misunderstood something?

The second version has a label switching problem: You can permute the (arbitrary) order of the 3 factors without changing the likelihood of the data and your priors are symmetric with respect to ordering. The first version does not have that problem because the factors are associated (up to measurement error) with particular observed variables.

Ben

First recode subFacs as

vector[3] subjFacs[N];

and then remove the loop and replace the first line with

subjFacs ~ multi_normal(zeroesForFacMeans, facCov);

and subsequent lines with something like this:

Y[ , 1] ~ normal(to_vector(subjFacs[ , 1]) + outcomeMeans[1], outcomeSds[1]);

The to_vector is ugly, but there's no good way to vectorize
both the multi_normal and the normal argument as it needs to be
an array for vectorization of multi_normal and a vector (for the vector arithmetic)
in the other. We need to generalize the way we do vectorization of
multi-normal, but never seem to be able to find the time.

- Bob

used to more conventionally formatted code.

> Ah, I have it there because when teaching others, I illustrate how you can use lkj_corr(x) with larger values of x to express more credibility at zero in the priors.

I'd say "around zero" rather than "at zero" because 0 is just
a point and has no credibility in and of itself. What it does
is concentrate the prior probabilty mass around the unit
correlation matrix.

> P.S. The unconventional spacing is very distracting to those of
> used to more conventionally formatted code.
>
> And here I thought that conversion of my tab-delimited to two-space-delimited was sufficient to satisfy the list's preferred format : P What spacing are you speaking of? The blank lines I use for grouping similar things?

Getting rid of tabs is a first step since they cause local rendering
chaos.

I find the spaces before semicolons and inside parens very distracting.
But then I read a ton of code all day and am super picky. We finally just
started using cpplint to validate our own C++ code style, though even that
doesn't pick up on everything. For instance, there's always space after a comma
and never space befroe a semicolon. Always spaces before left braces or
conditionals, so no "model{" or "if(" as we see a lot of. And never space before
function args, so "exp(3)" instead of the "exp (3)" we get from some R users.

- Bob

How is it switching position with second and third? I can see how this would happen if you have three factors all loading on all items, but each factor loads on unique items.

The only constraints are that each of the 3 factors has one positive loading with the rest unrestricted. Suppose those positive loadings are 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. parts:
I ran the model. I see the multimodality, but it's not due to factor switching. The sampler is essentially finding a mode that would otherwise assign all betas for certain factors to be negative (thus flipping the correlation between factors). In this case, the positive_betas[2:3] are pushing up against 0 and the non-constrained betas for those factors are negative. Basically, it's a bit like dropping an indicator from the model altogether and the latent variable is being defined by two indicators that load negatively on the factor. This is not the best model, of course, and you can tell it because the lp__ for the chains where it's finding a mode that essentially drops an indicator and lets the remaining ones be negative is less than the lp__ for the other chains.

The only way I see to fix this is to ensure all items are positively scaled and force all factor loadings to be positive. This is theoretically justifiable, in my opinion.

Also, go Stan! Fully Bayesian CFA model in 12 seconds is pretty great!

data{

  #N: number of subjects
  int N ;

  #K: number of outcomes per subject
  int K ;

  #Y: matrix of outcomes
  matrix[N,K] Y ;

}
transformed data{

  # zeroesForFacMeans: vector of zeroes for factor means
  vector[3] zeroesForFacMeans ;
  zeroesForFacMeans = rep_vector(0,3) ;

}
parameters{

  # facSds: SDs for the 3 latent factors
  vector<lower=0>[3] facSds ;

  # facCor: correlations amongst the 3 latent factors
  corr_matrix[3] facCor ;

  # subjFacs: matrix of values for each factor associated with each subject
  matrix[N,3] subjFacs ;

  # outcomeMeans: means for each outcome
  vector[9] outcomeMeans ;

  # outcomeSds: SDs for each outcome
  vector<lower=0>[9] outcomeSds ;

  # betas: how each factor loads on to each outcome.
  #        only 6 (rather than 9) because first beta
  #        for each factor set has been fixed at 1
  #        for identifiability
  vector[6] betas ;

}
transformed parameters{

  #facCov: covariance matrix for latent factors
  matrix[3,3] facCov ;
  facCov = quad_form_diag(facCor,facSds) ;

}

  facSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
  facCor ~ lkj_corr(1) ;
  outcomeMeans ~ normal(0,1) ;
  outcomeSds ~ weibull(2,1) ;
  betas ~ normal(0,1) ;

    Y[i,2] ~ normal( subjFacs[i,1]*betas[1] + outcomeMeans[2] , outcomeSds[2] ) ;

  }
